headline: Hacker fits 537,000 domains in a $5 ESP32 ad-blocking dongle with 10ms lookup speed
summary: An Egyptian developer created a hardware-based DNS ad-blocker using a $5 ESP32-C3 microcontroller, storing over half a million domains in just 4MB of flash memory.
details: A developer has engineered a hardware-based ad-blocking DNS filter using a $5 ESP32-C3 "SuperMini" board. This compact device can block over 500,000 domains with an impressive 10-millisecond lookup latency.

Created by Egyptian full-stack developer ZedAxis (@M-Abozaid), the project serves as a backup DNS for his home network, ensuring continuous ad-blocking even when his primary Pi-hole server is unavailable.
The ESP32-C3 used has limited specifications, featuring just 400KB of RAM and 4MB of flash memory. This constraint meant a plaintext blocklist was impractical due to its size.
To overcome memory limitations, ZedAxis employed a clever hashing trick. He uses 40-bit FNV-1a hashes to represent each domain, balancing collision rates with memory efficiency.

The build process involves downloading public blocklists, stripping duplicates, hashing each domain, sorting the resulting list, and writing it to the ESP32's flash memory. When a DNS query arrives, the device hashes the hostname and performs a binary search against the sorted hash table. The firmware uses only about 50KB of RAM.

A design compromise allows for maximum blocklist capacity: by disabling over-the-air (OTA) updates, the second firmware partition can be reclaimed for the blocklist database. This boosts the blocked domain count from around 250,000 to approximately 537,000.

This project is not intended to replace full-featured solutions like Pi-hole or AdGuard Home, which offer detailed statistics and extensive configuration options. Instead, it functions as a low-power, silent "insurance policy" for filtered DNS responses.
The device sips only a few dozen milliamps of power and can be conveniently powered from a USB port, such as one found on an ISP-provided router.

headline_marked: [[PC runs on 192 AA batteries]], successfully boots into Hannah Montana Linux
headline: PC runs on 192 AA batteries, successfully boots into Hannah Montana Linux
summary: The system proved stable during stress testing and even played FreeDoom, showcasing surprising performance for this unconventional power source.
details: Creator Uwoslab successfully built an interconnected power bank using 192 AA cells to run a modern AM4 system. This unconventional setup managed to boot a PC without compromising its performance.

The project began with an initial plan for 400 AA batteries, but Uwoslab ultimately wired 192 cells. These batteries were split across three laser-cut wooden boxes, each holding 64 cells, providing structural rigidity and connection points.

Previous attempts to power a PC with 9V zinc-carbon batteries failed due to instability. This experience led to the switch to 1.5V Alkaline batteries, specifically "high-drain" Pookell AA Alkaline cells, which provide the necessary 12V for stable operation when wired in series.

Crucially, the creator avoided traditional wall-plug power supplies and 12V-to-220V inverters. Instead, the parallel battery grid was run directly into a 12V DC-to-ATX adapter board, plugged straight into the motherboard.

The PC itself is an AM4 system, likely with a G-series chip as it lacks a dedicated GPU, and boots directly from a flash drive. It successfully booted into Hannah Montana Linux, a popular distro from 2009 that recently received a modern update.

The battery-powered PC ran for 30 minutes and passed the built-in Linux CPU stress test (stress-ng) with the CPU pegged at 98% usage. The CPU voltage remained stable at 11.95V, confirming the experiment's remarkable success.
